wa_buckner_mountain_north_face.name: Boston Basin, Sharkfin Col rappel, and south across the Boston Glacier to the schrund
wa_buckner_mountain_north_face.notes:
Start from the Boston Basin trailhead near 3,200 ft, about 21.7 miles up Cascade River Road — a different and shorter drive than the Cascade Pass trailhead used for the southwest route. The climbers' path follows an old overgrown mining road about a mile to a former mine site, then a steep boot path through old growth with roughly four creek crossings, emerging above treeline near 5,300 ft into Boston Basin: about 2.5 miles and 3,100 ft, typically three to four hours. Camp low at about 5,300 ft or high at 6,300-6,400 ft; NPS permit required and camping restricted to the established sites.

From high camp, follow the Quien Sabe Glacier route roped, and climb toward Sharkfin Col rather than taking the loose class 3-4 scramble around Boston Peak. Many parties gain the ridge just east of the col, where a natural or fixed sling anchor is used for a short rappel — or, in leaner conditions, a steep no-fall-zone downclimb on crumbly mixed rock — onto the Boston Glacier. Multiple trip reports flag this as the technical crux of the approach, sometimes harder than the climbing above.

Once on the Boston Glacier, rope up and traverse south toward the base of Buckner's north face, zig-zagging around the schrund and large crevasses near the toe, with some rock scrambling to bypass the gap. Many parties bivy on the glacier itself around 7,800 ft to shorten summit day.

A second way in reaches the same glacier over Sahale and the Boston-Sahale col from Sahale Glacier Camp.
wa_buckner_mountain_north_face.season: Late May through early July for the best face conditions
hazards: A short rappel or a steep no-fall-zone downclimb off Sharkfin Col on crumbly mixed rock — the crux of the approach, and it has to be reversed
A viciously crevassed upper Boston Glacier with cracks scattered randomly across the ice
A bergschrund at the toe of the face that can run its full width, needing rock scrambling to bypass
Wind-scoured ice on some ascents and moderate powder on others — the face's character changes completely with conditions
Cornices on the summit ridge, and rockfall as the day warms
wa_buckner_mountain_north_face.baseFinding:
The base is the bergschrund at the toe of the face, on the Boston Glacier, and the position test is directional: from the col you traverse south across the glacier. If you turned north you are heading for Forbidden's north side.

The entry move is a zig-zag and it is the positive test: work climber's left of the bergschrund, then back right into the centre of the lower face, and then straight up. Left, right, up. A party that crossed the schrund directly and started climbing where it stood has not found the line the face is climbed on.

What you are climbing confirms it: about 1,300 ft of 40-50 degree snow and ice, continuous, with no rock pitches. If you are on rock below the summit ridge, you have drifted off the face.

The finish is the other countable point, and getting it wrong costs time at the worst moment: continue straight up until upper rock cliffs force a rising traverse to the left. Then, within about 200 ft of the summit, go left around a craggy rock outcrop at the end of those cliffs, and only then back right to the top. Both moves are left. A party that goes right at the cliff band has misread the finish.

And the approach itself is the strongest negative test against this peak's other route: the Southwest Face is reached over Cascade Pass, Sahale Arm and Horseshoe Basin, on the opposite side of the mountain, and the two share no ground until the summit ridge. If you walked past an old mine in a basin at 7,000 ft, you are on the southwest route.

wa_prusik_peak_der_sportsman.name: Aasgard Pass and the Core, fifty feet left of the standard south-face line
camps: Perfection Lake and Inspiration Lake basin camps
wa_prusik_peak_der_sportsman.notes:
The Core Enchantments approach: Stuart Lake trailhead, Stuart Lake Trail 2.5 miles to the Colchuck Lake Trail junction, across Mountaineer Creek and up the switchbacks to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft. From the boulder field at the lake's south end, Aasgard Pass — 1.25 miles gaining about 2,000 ft of steep loose scree and dirt, the physical crux of the approach, with a hidden creek and moat under lingering snow into early July.

From the pass at 7,841 ft, continue cross-country through the upper Core past Isolation and Tranquil Lake toward Prusik Pass and Gnome Tarn. Parties commonly bivy at the tarn, about twenty minutes from the base. There is no maintained trail for the last stretch.

The Snow Lakes trail is the longer alternative when Aasgard or the trailhead is closed: past Nada and Snow Lakes to Lake Viviane, then up and right toward Temple Lake and up climbers' paths through boulders to the base of the south face.
wa_prusik_peak_der_sportsman.season: Roughly Jul-Sep; the route is a hard rock climb and wants dry, warm granite
hazards: Aasgard Pass: steep loose scree, with a hidden creek and moat under early-season snow and a fatal history
Avalanche exposure on the pass in shoulder season
Unmarked cross-country approach over slabs and talus in the Core
5.11+ crux on the first pitch, sustained hard crack climbing far above gear
Loose block in the finishing chimney
Mixed rappel anchors on the north side: one bolted station, then gear and slung naturals; carry webbing to back up old tat
Afternoon thunderstorms; Core Zone camping needs a permit
wa_prusik_peak_der_sportsman.baseFinding:
Fifty feet left of the standard South Face route. That is the published position and it is a pace count, not a description — find the classic line at the middle of the base of the face, then walk left about fifty feet.

The first pitch is the check, and it is a brutal one. This route's opening pitch is 5.11+. The line fifty feet to your right opens at 5.6 or 5.7 in a chimney. There is no ambiguity between those two pieces of climbing: if you are cruising your first pitch, you are on the wrong route, and if you are fighting a tipsy crux entering a stembox, you are on this one.

What the first pitch looks like from the ground, so you can commit before you leave the deck: an easy, unappealing left-slanting crack system leading up to a stance below an obvious stembox. The unremarkable start is deceptive and is exactly why the fifty-foot offset matters — the interesting rock is not visible from the base.

Belay confirmation: pitch one ends at a two-bolt anchor after liebacking and stemming up the right of twin cracks. Most of this face is natural gear; arriving at bolts is strong evidence you are on this line rather than on a neighbour.

And the named pitch higher up: an undercling flake pitch that parties call the money pitch, then a committing corner where the route switches cracks. If you never leave one crack for another, you have wandered onto adjoining ground.

Descent note that affects the approach decision: this one rappels the north side in five, then needs one more rappel from the balanced-rock landmark at the base of the West Ridge to get back down to your packs.

wa_prusik_peak_der_sportsman.name: Snow Lakes and the lower Enchantments

bivy.name: Perfection Lake and Inspiration Lake basin camps
bivy.notes: The natural base for Prusik Peak's West Ridge and South Face, putting the approach at well under an hour of walking and scrambling to Prusik Pass. Most parties reach it over Aasgard Pass from Colchuck Lake, which is a steep loose grind with a heavy pack rather than a trail in any real sense. Camp on rock, sand or gravel and stay off the heather — the meadows here recover very slowly. No fires at any elevation in the basin.
bivy.water: Reliable — the chain of lakes and the connecting streams hold water all season
bivy.permit: Core Enchantment zone. This is the hardest overnight permit in the area to draw; the advance lottery through recreation.gov is the main route in, with a small number of Core spots also released in the geofenced daily lottery at Leavenworth. A Core permit is the flexible one — it is valid for camping in any of the five zones (Core, Colchuck, Snow, Stuart, Eightmile/Caroline).
bivy.capacity: Numerous hardened sites on granite benches and sand between the two lakes; the whole Core zone is held to roughly two dozen people a night, so it is never crowded once you are in

bivy.name: Gnome Tarn
bivy.notes: The tarn sits almost directly under Prusik's south side and gives the shortest approach of anywhere to the South Face routes and the West Ridge. Getting there means leaving the main basin route and scrambling up from around Perfection Lake toward Prusik Pass on a faint, easily lost path over granite. It is exposed and high, so a night here can be considerably colder and windier than the lakes below. The camping is on rock, which is both the right surface to use and the reason a level spot takes some hunting.
bivy.water: The tarn itself, though it is small and can drop low or silty late in a dry season; the lakes below are the fallback
bivy.permit: Core Enchantment zone, same permit and same lottery reality as the Perfection Lake camps. There is no separate allocation for climbers and no exemption for a single night below a route.
bivy.capacity: A handful of small sites on slab and sand; realistically one or two parties before it feels crowded

wa_prusik_peak_der_sportsman.notes: The longer, more gradual way in from Icicle Creek Road: the Snow Lakes trail climbs past Nada and Snow lakes to Lake Vivianne, about ten miles with well over 5,000 ft of gain, looking straight at Prusik's south face. From Vivianne continue past the upper lakes to the base of the south face. It avoids the loose grind of Aasgard Pass at the cost of roughly two more miles and a thousand more feet.
hazards: Long approach of about ten miles and well over 5,000 ft of gain via the Snow Lakes trail to Lake Viviane
Unmarked cross-country travel past the upper lakes to the base of the south face
5.11+ crux on the first pitch, sustained hard crack climbing far above gear
Loose block in the finishing chimney
Mixed rappel anchors on the north side: one bolted station, then gear and slung naturals; carry webbing to back up old tat
Afternoon thunderstorms; Core Zone camping needs a permit

wa_prusik_peak_south_face_burgner_stanle.name: Aasgard Pass to Gnome Tarn
camps: Perfection Lake and Inspiration Lake basin camps
wa_prusik_peak_south_face_burgner_stanle.notes:
Stuart Lake Trailhead, Colchuck Lake Trail #1599A across Mountaineer Creek and up the switchbacks to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft — about four miles and 2,000-2,200 ft.

From the boulder field at the lake's south end, climb Aasgard Pass: roughly 2,000 ft in a little over a mile of loose scree and dirt, and the crux of the day. Stay climber's left of the cliff bands; the terrain to climber's right, toward the waterfalls on Colchuck Peak's flank, cliffs out and has killed people. Snow lingering into early July hides a creek running beneath the talus.

From the pass at 7,841 ft travel cross-country through the Core, dropping from Talisman Lake toward Rune Lake, then ascending to the gentle ridge east of Rune's upper basin to reach Gnome Tarn. Gnome Tarn is the standard camp for this face and sits close under it.

A longer approach on the Snow Lakes Trail exists and is the fallback when Aasgard or the Stuart Lake trailhead is closed; some parties deliberately go in over Aasgard and out via Snow Lakes, about 21 miles, to spare their knees a second descent of the pass.

The last stretch to the wall is unmarked cross-country over slabs and talus.
wa_prusik_peak_south_face_burgner_stanle.season: Jul-Sep; earlier the pass is a snow climb and the Core travel is on snow
hazards: Aasgard Pass: terrain to climber's right cliffs out, loose rock, fatalities on record
Hidden creek beneath the talus on the pass under early-season snow
Avalanche exposure on the pass in shoulder season
Unmarked cross-country slab and talus travel from Gnome Tarn to the base
Loose rock near the chockstone tunnel and runout sections on the upper flare and chimney pitches
North-side rappels on climber-built slung anchors; bring cordage; the line backs up when busy
Afternoon thunderstorms and party traffic on a very popular line
wa_prusik_peak_south_face_burgner_stanle.baseFinding:
From Gnome Tarn, traverse northeast to the south face. The base of the Stanley-Burgner sits at about 7,350 ft.

The defining feature is a pair of deep chimneys on the face. The route starts to the left of those two chimneys, in a crack system on steep white granite — the base is immediately beside a left-slanting chimney. Two deep chimneys with the route just left of them is the pattern to hold in your head; if you have walked past the chimneys and are still looking, you are right of the start.

The second confirmation is vegetation. The first pitch is 5.8 up the crack system and finishes at a belay just below some shrubby pines. From the talus, a photograph-worthy way to say it is that the route starts at the trees on the left and goes up. Pitch 2 then works up through those pines at 5.7. So: white granite, left of the two deep chimneys, aiming for a small stand of scrubby pines about a pitch up.

This face carries several routes that share the same base area and the same north-side rappel descent, so being one crack system over is easy and consequential. If your first pitch is harder than 5.8 or has no pines above it, you are on a neighbour.

Note that the West Ridge starts somewhere else entirely — around at Prusik Pass on the far side of the peak — so the two are not confusable at the base, only on the map.

wa_rock_mountain_west_route.name: Trail #1587 from US-2 to the Nason Ridge crest
wa_rock_mountain_west_route.notes: One of the steepest maintained trails near Stevens Pass, and it starts working immediately. From the dirt pullout on the north side of the highway the tread climbs on an old service road beneath powerlines, leaves the roadbed at a signed bend about a third of a mile up, and then runs into ninety-odd tight switchbacks on an open south-facing slope with no shade at all. Schilling Creek near the bottom is the only accessible water on the climb and it drops away quickly, so fill everything at the car and carry three litres or more. The grade eases into heather meadows around 2.8 miles and the tread tops out on the crest at about 6,000 ft. An alternate approach comes up the Snowy Creek trail from the Smithbrook road and joins the ridge higher.
wa_rock_mountain_west_route.season: Late June to October; snow lingers
hazards: Ninety-odd tight switchbacks on an open south-facing slope with no shade; heat and sun load
No reliable water above the creek low down; carry 3+ liters
Loose rock and jumbled talus on the upper ridge and final scramble
North-facing snow patch below the summit ridge can persist into fall and goes slick by afternoon
Cornice or residual snow on the narrow connecting ridge into early summer
Afternoon thunderstorms on a wholly exposed crest
Habituated mountain goats near the summit; keep your distance
wa_rock_mountain_west_route.baseFinding: Two signed junctions bracket the start of the scrambling and neither is the base by itself. The first is where the trail tops out on the crest at roughly 6,000 ft and meets the Nason Ridge trail; turn left along the ridge here, since the right-hand branch drops away toward a lake overlook. The second, about half a mile on, is where the Snowy Creek trail joins from the south — that is the alternate approach, not your line, and past it the constructed tread stops being tread and thins into a path over loose jumbled talus. That change underfoot is the base. From there the crest runs over a false south summit first; it carries no structure on it. The true summit beyond is identified by the stone foundation of the old fire lookout, and the short connecting ridge between the two is narrow enough to want care and can hold a cornice or old snow into early summer. If you are standing on a high point with nothing built on it and the ridge carries on, keep going.

wa_rock_mountain_west_route.name: Snowy Creek trail from Smith Brook road

bivy.name: Nason Creek Campground and the Lake Wenatchee drive-in camps
bivy.notes: The drive-in base for the whole ridge, and the honest recommendation for most parties climbing these peaks: all four summits are day objectives from the highway trailheads, and sleeping at a developed campground with water and driving fifteen or twenty minutes to a trailhead beats carrying an overnight load up two thousand feet of dry switchbacks. The season runs roughly May through mid-October. From here the Merritt Lake and Round Mountain trailheads are a short drive west and north along the highway and its spurs, with Rock Mountain and Snowy Creek further west toward the pass. It is also the sensible place to reorganise mid-trip: a party that has come off the crest at one end and needs to reposition to the other has this corridor to do it in. Note that the trailheads themselves have very limited parking — Rock Mountain and Snowy Creek in particular hold only a few cars — so an early start from a nearby campground is worth more here than the extra sleep of staying further out.
bivy.water: Piped potable water at the developed campgrounds through the operating season, and Nason Creek itself alongside. This is the one place where water is a non-issue, which is why every party working this ridge should fill everything here before driving up to a trailhead rather than counting on anything above.
bivy.permit: A per-night fee, currently around the high twenties at the forest campground, with advance reservations opening well ahead and closing a few days before arrival. The state park campgrounds have their own reservation system and their own fee. No wilderness permit is involved anywhere in this zone. Fire restrictions apply in the campgrounds through the summer and are commonly total bans in late season.
bivy.capacity: Nason Creek is the closest and largest, laid out over four loops on both sides of the highway near the southeastern end of Lake Wenatchee, taking vehicles up to about thirty-five feet. Roughly sixty percent of sites are reservable in advance and the remainder are first come, first served. The state park campgrounds around the lake add substantially more capacity, and there are further national forest campgrounds spread along the highway corridor.

bivy.name: Rock Lake
bivy.notes: The camp for Rock Mountain and the western anchor of the whole crest. The Rock Mountain trail leaves US 2 at about 2,650 feet and is relentless — roughly 3,400 feet in four miles of endless switchbacks on a hot, open, south-facing slope with no water and very little shade, which is the single most quoted complaint about this peak. The lake sits in a basin below the summit ridge, so a party that has ground up the trail can drop packs, camp, and take the northeast ridge and the summit unencumbered. Most people do Rock Mountain in a day; camping here is what you do when the heat has beaten you, when you are starting the Nason Ridge traverse rather than finishing it, or when you want the summit at first light. The alternative approach by the Snowy Creek trail from the forest road on the north side starts higher and climbs less, and it is the kinder line in warm weather, though the road is brushy. Snow lingers on the upper slopes into early summer and the basin holds it later than the trail below. West of the lake, the crest trail toward Crescent Lake has badly eroded steep sidehill sections with little tread left, and that stretch is the crux of moving along this ridge with a pack.
bivy.water: The lake, and it is the first water of any kind on the Rock Mountain trail — the entire climb from the highway is dry. It holds all season. Treat it, because the shoreline is well used and the basin is small. Fill here for everything you intend to do on the crest, since the next dependable source westward or eastward is Crescent Lake, and the ridge between the two carries nothing.
bivy.permit: None. Nason Ridge sits outside the Alpine Lakes Wilderness, so there is no wilderness permit, no self-issue slip, no quota and no lottery anywhere. The Rock Mountain trailhead has very limited parking, though no fee is charged there and the Merritt Lake end requires no pass either; of the trailheads serving this crest only Nason Ridge is a fee site, at $5 a day or $30 a year. Campfires are prohibited above 5,000 feet in this national forest, which covers this camp and every other high site here, and summer burn bans are routine on this dry east-side ground.
bivy.capacity: Several pleasant established sites around the lake, enough for two or three parties; small and it feels small, with no facilities

wa_rock_mountain_west_route.notes: Drive Smith Brook road six miles and the narrow, brushy Snowy Creek road a further three and a half to a small trailhead with very limited parking. The trail follows Snowy Creek through old growth, then climbs to the crest and joins the main route about half a mile short of the summit. It is shorter and far less steep than the highway trail. The Snowy Creek road has been closed by storm damage since June 2026, so check before driving it.

wa_mount_logan_fremont_glacier.name: Park Creek Pass and the heather traverse to the Fremont saddle and the hogsback
camps: Meadows north of Park Creek Pass
Valley camps on the walk in
wa_mount_logan_fremont_glacier.notes:
The standard start is the Colonial Creek Campground trailhead on SR-20 near milepost 130, about 1,060-1,200 ft, and the Thunder Creek trail south for roughly 16-18 miles to the Thunder Basin camp area around 6,000 ft and on to Park Creek Pass. A southern alternative reaches the same pass from Stehekin: the High Bridge guard station near 1,600 ft, the Stehekin River trail to the Park Creek trailhead, then the Park Creek trail past Buckner Camp — with a creek crossing on a less-than-substantial footlog that is genuinely nerve-wracking in the dark.

From Park Creek Pass leave the maintained trail and traverse gradually northward around a broad ridge through open heather and high alpine terrain, roughly a mile and a half to two miles, crossing a rib around 7,600 ft and a steep gully through cliff bands around 7,350 ft that can hold snow or ice. That brings you to the Fremont Glacier saddle around 8,000-8,250 ft, where rock-outcrop bivy sites with nearby running water make the standard high camp.

From camp it is about three and a half hours to the summit.
hazards: Crevasses on the Fremont Glacier, generally small but present
Bergschrund opens below the summit ridge late season as the snow finger melts, plus a moat at the crest
Exposed, often unroped Class 3-4 scrambling on the summit ridge
Steep gully through cliff bands near 7,350 ft can hold snow or ice
Long unmaintained cross-country route-finding above the moraine camp
Hazardous footlog crossings over Thunder Creek at night or high water; no fixed anchors for rappels
wa_mount_logan_fremont_glacier.baseFinding:
The base is the Hogsback — the snow spine at the upper edge of the Fremont Glacier, on the peak's south ridge. You reach it by a gentle glacier crossing from the saddle camp, and there is a moat crossing to step from the snow onto the crest, which late in the season may have no bridge left at all. Snow spine plus a gap to step across is the confirmation you are at the start.

Then count three features in order, and the order is the whole route-finding problem: a class 3-4 rock pitch gains a left-slanting ramp — a fault-line weakness in the cliff bands — to the summit ridge; then exposed class 2-3 ledges on the east side of the ridge lead through a U-notch between the summit tower and the south horn; then a final class 3-4 pitch of about 100 ft on good holds and solid rock reaches the tiny summit.

The strongest negative test is the ramp: if you are trying to climb the summit tower directly from the glacier, you have missed it. The ramp is the way through the cliff bands and it slants left. Going straight at the tower puts you on ground the route deliberately avoids.

The U-notch is the second confirmation and it is a shape, not a height: a U-shaped gap between the summit tower and the south horn, reached by traversing ledges on the ridge's east flank. If you never dropped onto the east side, you did not take the ledges.

And know which side of the mountain you are on before you start: this is the southeast/southwest approach, from Park Creek Pass. The Douglas Glacier route comes from Easy Pass and the Douglas Creek alder on the northeast; the Banded Glacier route comes from Fisher Creek and gains the northeast ridge at about 8,800 ft. All three finish on the same summit block and share nothing below it.

wa_mount_logan_fremont_glacier.name: Stehekin and the Park Creek trail to Park Creek Pass

bivy.name: Moraine camp above the pass
bivy.notes: Roughly 6,350 ft, gained by turning east from the meadows and climbing about 500 ft into the moraine of the glacier remnant. Flat, sandy and better protected than the open meadows, and the usual high camp for the Fremont Glacier. From here the route traverses about two miles north around a broad ridge over heather and rock to reach the glacier near 8,000 ft.
bivy.water: Snowmelt off the glacier remnant beside the moraine
bivy.permit: Inside the park; covered by the same backcountry permit as the rest of the route
bivy.capacity: A sheltered flat big enough for a few tents

bivy.name: Meadows north of Park Creek Pass
bivy.notes: Broad sandy meadows a short way north of Park Creek Pass, which itself sits near 6,100 ft. This is where the long valley walk finally ends and the climbing terrain starts; parties either stop here or push the last 500 ft into the moraine above.
bivy.water: Creeks and snowmelt in the meadows below the pass
bivy.permit: Everything on this route is inside North Cascades National Park, so an overnight needs a park backcountry permit and the itinerary is built night by night from designated camps and cross-country zones
bivy.capacity: Open flat ground rather than built sites; a few parties at a time

bivy.name: Valley camps on the walk in
bivy.notes: The approach is long enough that most parties sleep at least one night in the forest before reaching climbing terrain — Thunder Basin in the upper Thunder Creek drainage from the Colonial Creek side, or Buckner Camp on Park Creek (named for the mountain, not on it) coming in from Stehekin. Park Creek has to be crossed near some of these camps and is worth doing in daylight.
bivy.water: Thunder Creek and Park Creek run beside these camps
bivy.permit: Designated North Cascades camps, reserved by name for specific nights on the backcountry permit; Stehekin-side parties can obtain the permit at the ranger station there
bivy.capacity: Established backcountry sites with a fixed number of parties each

wa_mount_logan_fremont_glacier.notes: From the Park Creek Trailhead on the Stehekin Valley Road, the Park Creek trail climbs to Park Creek Pass and joins the Thunder Creek line there. It needs the Lake Chelan boat and the Stehekin shuttle to reach the trailhead.

Steep gully through cliff bands near 7,350 ft above Park Creek Pass can hold snow or ice
Crevasses on the Fremont Glacier, generally small but present

wa_tenpeak_mountain_southeast.name: White River Trail #1507 and the old sheep path into Thunder Basin
wa_tenpeak_mountain_southeast.notes: From Coles Corner take Hwy 207 toward Lake Wenatchee, then White River Road (FR-6400) to its end at the White River / Indian Creek Trailhead near 2,300 ft. Hike White River Trail #1507 about six miles to the Thunder Creek crossing; there is an established camp right at the crossing. Half a mile past Thunder Creek the maintained trail is left behind for an old, unmaintained sheep path that climbs the west side of the Thunder Creek drainage. This is the hard part of the walk in: avalanche debris, blowdown, and dense slide alder choking the tread below the lower basin. Above the alder it opens into a lower basin near 4,175 ft and then climbs steeply into Thunder Basin, an open basin of granite slabs and small tarns which is the standard high camp and has a direct view of the peak. The flat upper basin is near 5,200 ft; the granite slabs and two small tarns at the top of the basin, near 6,400-6,500 ft, are a higher camp closer to the col. A far longer alternative comes in from the west — North Fork Sauk Trail #649 past Mackinaw Shelter to the PCT, then cross-country over Boulder Pass and through the Napeequa to the peak's north and north-east side. Parties who have done it report twenty-plus stream crossings and heavy brush over three days. It is a different trip, not a shortcut.
wa_tenpeak_mountain_southeast.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, while the snow between camp and the col is still continuous enough to walk and the summit rock is dry
hazards: Loose, rotten rock in the summit gully and the broken chimney above it, directly over anyone belaying below
Dense slide alder choking the old sheep path below the lower basin — the slowest half-mile of the approach by a wide margin
Crevasses on the small hanging glaciers crossed on the northern approach variations
Cornices and wind-loaded slopes on the approach ridgelines into early summer
White River Road has a repeated history of flash-flood washouts, so the drive is the first thing to verify
wa_tenpeak_mountain_southeast.baseFinding:
The col east of the summit block is the base, and the thing that confirms it is the wind. Parties who have stood there describe it as an incredibly windy notch below the east face — it is a gap on a ridge, so it funnels, and on a Cascade summit day you will feel it before you can see anything.

Getting there is a single bearing from camp: from Thunder Basin cross talus and snow toward the col that sits east of the summit block, near 8,000 ft. Crampons and an axe are normal for the snow, which stays firm in the morning. You are aiming for the gap beside the summit tower, not for the tower.

The positive test for the start of the climbing: from the col the route takes a loose gully on the left for about 85 ft to a ledge system. Loose first, ledge second. If the first thing above the col is clean solid rock, or if you are moving right rather than left, you are not on it.

The second confirmation is a crack. Above the ledge system the finish is a broken chimney with a good jam crack running up it, and that crack is the one genuinely positive hold-bearing feature on the summit block. Class 4 to easy fifth depending on conditions. If you are on a face with no chimney and no crack, you have drifted off the ledge system.

What it is not: this is a short summit block, not a wall. From the col to the top is roughly two rope lengths. If you have been climbing for hours above the col you are not on this route.

Rack and rock: everything from the col up is loose. Helmet, and space the party out — the gully drops what the leader pulls straight onto whoever is below.

wa_lincoln_peak_standard.name: Middle Fork Nooksack Road (FR-38) and Rankin Creek to the treeline camp, then the southwest basin
wa_lincoln_peak_standard.notes:
This is the more direct way to the X Couloir: from the south via the Middle Fork Nooksack River Road (FR-38). The southwest face can also be reached from Heliotrope Ridge through the Thunder Glacier cirque, a less direct line with more glacier travel; do not confuse either with the north-facing Coleman side, which leads to the other route on this mountain.

Drive FR-38 toward its mile-12.5 switchback and start walking the old decommissioned road around Point 4481 toward Rankin Creek. Snow travel — often by bike or snowshoe on the lower stretch — leads past East Rankin Lake near 5,120 ft and up into the basin to a sheltered camp at treeline around 6,100 ft, by the highest trees in the basin below Seward Peak. Roughly seven miles and 3,350 ft of gain to camp.

Access: FR-38, damaged in the December 2025 floods, has been closed to vehicles at milepost 7 by a washout since July 27, 2026, with no end date given on the Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest alert still posted on September 26, 2026, and a separate gate at Wallace Creek near mile 10 closes the road 1 December to 15 June for elk calving. Confirm the drivable road-end with the Mount Baker Ranger District before the trip; the length of the approach varies year to year.
wa_lincoln_peak_standard.season: Roughly Apr-Jun. A spring snow climb; essentially never done in summer, because what makes it climbable is continuous snow rather than the rubble underneath
hazards: FR-38 flood damage with no repair timeline, plus an elk-calving gate closed 1 Dec to 15 Jun, so the approach length varies
Bergschrund crossing (AI3+ on 70-85 degree snow and ice) that must be done cold and early
About 1,500 ft of 30-40 degree snow with a steep serac step, all above a long runout
Notoriously loose, rotten volcanic rock; the gully funnels rockfall and spindrift after storms
Wet-snow instability and rapid softening on the southwest-facing line as it warms
Descent is a real rappel sequence off pickets and slung horns, not a walk-off
Complex route-finding among the Black Buttes
wa_lincoln_peak_standard.baseFinding:
The highest trees in the basin are the camp, and the camp is the last thing you can navigate to. Above treeline the southwest side of Lincoln is open snow and there is nothing to hold on to in cloud. So the arrival marker is vegetative rather than topographic: climb until the trees stop, and camp at the last of them, below Seward Peak, around 6,100 ft.

The bergschrund is the base of the climb. From camp an alpine start takes you into the southwest basin and to the schrund while the snow is still cold and firm. Above it is roughly 1,500 ft of 30-40 degree snow with a steep serac step in it.

Do not expect one clean couloir — this is the trap the name sets. Parties who have climbed and skied it describe it as less a couloir and more a series of steep chutes and faces, and the line drops from the high point to the highest notch, then down a narrow chute, and trends right out of view. So 'find the obvious couloir' is the wrong instruction and will have you standing in the basin looking for something that is not there. Work from the notch downward: the correct line is the one that connects to the highest notch on the skyline, and it is narrow where it leaves the basin.

The serac step is the confirmation. Somewhere in that 1,500 ft you meet a steep serac step. A line with no ice step in it is not the X Couloir.

And the aspect settles the coarse error: this route faces southwest and this approach reaches it from Rankin Creek. If you are standing on the Coleman Glacier looking at a shaded north-facing cirque, you are under the other route on this mountain.

wa_lincoln_peak_standard.name: Heliotrope Ridge and the Thunder Glacier cirque
wa_lincoln_peak_standard.notes: Start at the Heliotrope Ridge trailhead and follow the trail toward the old cabin site, then rope up and cross the lower glaciers south into the Thunder Glacier cirque to reach the southwest side of the peak. It is less direct than the Rankin Creek line, with much more glacier travel, but it starts from a paved-to-gravel road that is usually open when the Middle Fork road is not.
hazards: Roped glacier travel across the lower glaciers into the Thunder Glacier cirque, with more glacier travel than the Rankin Creek line
Crevasse and serac hazard on the approach glaciers
Bergschrund crossing (AI3+ on 70-85 degree snow and ice) that must be done cold and early
About 1,500 ft of 30-40 degree snow with a steep serac step above a long runout
Notoriously loose, rotten volcanic rock; the gully funnels rockfall and spindrift after storms
Wet-snow instability and rapid softening on the southwest-facing line as it warms
Descent is a real rappel sequence; going back north toward Heliotrope Ridge from a Rankin camp puts a glacier between you and camp

wa_cosho_peak_scramble.name: Cosho Camp to the 7,830 ft saddle and the north snowfield
wa_cosho_peak_scramble.notes: From Cosho Camp continue west down the Fisher Creek Trail about a mile and leave it at one of the gullies due south of the Cosho-Kimtah saddle, starting around 3,800 ft. The climb up is the crux of the day: sustained bushwhacking through trees and brush for the first thousand feet, then loose, tedious scree and steep grass with occasional solid rock, roughly 4,000 ft of gain to the saddle at about 7,830 ft. Parties combining Cosho with Kimtah come the other way instead, descending Kimtah's south gully and following cairns down the connecting traverse to the same saddle.
hazards: Four thousand feet of loose, brushy off-trail gain with no water above the creek
Firm snow on the north side of the saddle — carry an ice axe
Remote and rarely visited; navigating back to the correct gully in poor visibility is the real danger
The wrong gully on the way down leads into brush
wa_cosho_peak_scramble.baseFinding: At the saddle, cross to the north side and climb snow until it runs out. From the 7,830 ft saddle the route does not follow the crest: step over onto the snowfield on the north side and climb moderate snow northwest to roughly 8,100 ft. Where the snow ends is the base of the climbing — a couple of hundred feet of third-class rock on the upper east face, reported mostly solid, with cairns marking the stretches where the ground is ambiguous, finishing at the summit. That snow-to-rock transition at about 8,100 ft is the test. If you are still on talus and scree on the south side of the saddle with no snowfield below you, you have not crossed over. If you are working up a broad crest with no snow anywhere, you are on the wrong saddle: the correct one lies due north of the point at which you left the Fisher Creek Trail, between Cosho and Kimtah.

wa_emerald_peak_west_route.name: North Fork Entiat Trail #1437 to the meadow camp
camps: The basin between Emerald and Saska, and Milham Pass
Cottonwood Camp and the Entiat River road campgrounds
Fox Camp, North Fork Entiat trail
wa_emerald_peak_west_route.notes: Drive the Entiat River Road and then the switchbacking forest-road spur to the North Fork Entiat Trailhead, and follow North Fork Entiat River Trail #1437 up-valley. Almost all of the distance to the peak is on trail. The usual staging point is the trail camp in the meadow below the summit around 6,700 ft, and the climb starts from the tread a short way north of it. A boat-access alternative exists on the far side, reaching the peak from Emerald Park via Trail #1230 out of the lakeshore settlement; it is a genuine second way in, but where that line joins the climbing is unclear, so the base-finding below is written for the trail camp side.
wa_emerald_peak_west_route.season: Mid-July into early October. Snow can hold in the gullies well into the season, and an axe is worth carrying early and mid-season.
hazards: Deep loose scree with a dug-in boot path; kicked rock runs onto parties below, so spread out and wear a helmet
Several gullies, correct one hidden until you round a buttress
Small summit area becomes exposed within a few paces of its centre
South point is a steeply inclined slab; a slip runs down the East Face
Nearby sub-summits are convincing and have been tagged by mistake
No water beyond the meadow
Remote, minimal cell coverage
wa_emerald_peak_west_route.baseFinding: The small boggy meadow where the trail turns sharply left is the departure. From the meadow camp, follow the tread north until it turns sharply left at a small boggy meadow around 6,900 ft — past that turn the trail carries on around the south shoulder of the neighbouring peak, which is not where you are going. Leave it there and climb north, or slightly east of due north, over open ground almost to the ridge crest between the two peaks. Just before the crest, look for a scree and talus slope leading up and to the right to a notch on the northwest ridge. Take that about halfway, then cut right and south into the adjacent gully, and climb it to the depression between the two summits. Expect to see several gullies on the way in and not the one you want: it stays hidden until you round a buttress, and cairns only start marking the way once you are past that corner. The true summit is the north point, to the left of the depression as you arrive. Do not use a register to settle which point you are on — parties have found none on either.

wa_emerald_peak_west_route.name: Emerald Park trail from Lucerne

bivy.name: The basin between Emerald and Saska, and Milham Pass
bivy.notes: The high camp for the crest traverse, about a mile and a half beyond Fox Camp on the Pyramid trail, in the basin that separates Emerald Peak from Saska Peak. This is where a party stages to link Cardinal, Emerald, Saska and Pinnacle Mountain in a single push over Milham Pass at about 6,663 ft, which is the classic way to do these four and much the most efficient. From the basin you climb to the upper shelf just below the ridge between Emerald and Saska and pick up the broad gully to the summit. Cardinal is the highest of the group and the furthest, and it is the one that turns a two-day plan into three. The setting is superb and the ground is loose — expect scree and blocky scrambling rather than clean rock, and expect the descents to take longer than the ascents. Season is short at this height in a heavy year, realistically mid-July to early October, and the reason to come late is the larch and the reason not to is the water. Weigh that honestly: an August party that finds the tarns dry has a long, hot walk back down to fix it. Weather moves in from the west with little warning here and the basin is fully exposed.
bivy.water: Snowmelt tarns and rivulets in the basin, and these are the crux of the whole plan. They are dependable in early and mid summer, unreliable by mid-August, and in a dry year they are gone entirely by late August, at which point the nearest certain water is back down at Fox Camp. Do not commit to a high camp here in late season without either confirming water or carrying it up. Milham Pass itself has none.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue, party limit of twelve. Camp on durable ground and well back from the tarns. No campfires — forest-wide restrictions aside, there is no fuel at this elevation and the ground is fragile. The trails in have been closed by the Little Giant Fire closure; check the Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest for current closures before you go.
bivy.capacity: A small number of tent-sized spots on benches and moraine in the upper basin; two or three parties at most, and less if you want flat ground

wa_emerald_peak_west_route.notes: Take the boat up Lake Chelan to Lucerne, follow the Domke Lake trail to the Emerald Park trail, and climb up Emerald Park to Milham Pass, which drops into the basin between Emerald and Saska. A boat-dependent alternative to the Entiat side, and the natural choice when coming from Lake Chelan.
hazards: Approach trails affected by a wildfire closure; check status before going
Boat-dependent access from Lake Chelan
Rockfall and loose rock in the erosion-carved west gully
Exposure on the south summit slab toward the East Face
Basin tarns unreliable by mid-August; camp fully exposed to weather from the west
Remote, minimal cell coverage

wa_mount_fernow_southeast_face.name: Phelps Creek and Leroy Basin, over the col and across the Gloomy Glacier
wa_mount_fernow_southeast_face.notes:
Same walk in as for Seven Fingered Jack and Maude: Phelps Creek trail to the Leroy Creek crossing at about 4,140 ft, then the steep unmaintained climbers' trail on the north side of the creek into Leroy Basin at about 6,100 ft.

This is the common approach but not the elegant one. It exists because the alternative is the ferry up Lake Chelan to Holden and the Railroad Creek trail into Copper Basin, which gains the East Ridge — the standard route — much more directly. A third option starts at Cottonwood on the Entiat River and reaches the East Ridge by way of the Entiat Glacier. All three converge on the same south-east face finish.

From Leroy Basin, head north-west toward a waterfall and climb its left side to a small notch on the ridge of Seven Fingered Jack. Published descriptions of this saddle vary — one places it just west of an obvious 7,700 ft col with a couple of bivy sites at the low point, another gives it as a notch reached past a second creek crossing — and they may or may not be the same feature, so check it on a map rather than assuming.

From the saddle you must drop about a thousand feet into the moraine at the terminus of the Gloomy Glacier, and every foot of it has to be regained on the way out. Two published ways down: descend to the tarn below and go around a prominent rock formation that guards the basin, or descend to the right across sandy ledges and down large boulders.

Expect roughly nine hours round trip from Leroy Basin, and a very long day car to car — one party left the trailhead at three in the morning and got back at eleven at night.
wa_mount_fernow_southeast_face.season: Roughly Jul-Sep; the Leroy-to-Gloomy crossing runs through avalanche terrain earlier than that
hazards: Route-finding is the crux: Fernow is not visible from Leroy Basin and cairns are sparse
About a thousand feet of descent from the col into the Gloomy basin that must be regained on the way out
Open crevasses and icy slopes at the Gloomy Glacier remnant; rope up or give it a wide berth
Avalanche terrain on the Leroy-to-Gloomy crossing earlier in the season
Roughly two thousand feet of exceptionally loose talus and scree above the basin
Exposed gravel-covered sloped slab traverse (about 30 m drop) and narrow exposed ledges off the col; avoidable
Exposed class 4 (occasionally low 5th) moves on the final summit block
Afternoon thunderstorms on the open upper ridge
wa_mount_fernow_southeast_face.baseFinding:
Fernow is not visible from Leroy basin, and this is confirmed rather than folklore. Parties climbing the basin under the cirque of Seven Fingered Jack report having real difficulty identifying the route because the peak simply is not in view. Do not stand in the basin trying to pick your line off the mountain; you cannot see it. Carry a track.

The arrival test is short and physical: cross the moraine below the Gloomy Glacier, go up the waterfall, and you are in the broad basin below Fernow. That is where the climbing starts.

Above that basin there are two decision points and both have a wrong answer that is on record.

First: descend the glacier to its terminal moraine at about 6,500 ft, then climb the right side of a stream to an upper snow-filled basin, and from there go south-west up a broad gully that turns eastward. That is Class 2-3 and gives you the luxury of knowing where you are. The alternative — dropping only to 7,000 ft and making a rising traverse through a succession of gullies, ribs and small cliffs — is Class 3-plus with snow and ice and the feeling of being lost somewhere in the Entiat Mountains.

Second, and this is the one that matters: from the broad gully, do not go all the way to the col and traverse the south-east face on the narrow ledges there. They are described as exposed enough to frighten a bird, with the honest observation that a fallen body would be unlikely to be found. Instead climb the broad gully to about 8,400 ft, then a loose gully to about 9,000 ft, and traverse the face at nine thousand on a wide ledge that is not exposed at all.

The 8,400 ft mark is a real landmark rather than a number on a map — two independent parties record the ground changing character there, one of them at a large bench holding permanent snow with water running off it. From 8,400 the line goes up loose talus to the ridge between Seven Fingered Jack and Fernow, where cairns pick up and weave around to the south-east ridge of the summit block. The cairns are reported by three separate parties, though one notes they stop near the summit itself.

The general principle behind all of it: climb as far as you can up the ridge separating Fernow's south-east and south-west faces. Once on the East Ridge, a couple of hundred feet of Class 3 on reasonably solid rock finishes it.

wa_mount_fernow_southeast_face.name: Holden Village and Copper Basin
wa_mount_fernow_southeast_face.notes: From Holden Village up to the Copper–Entiat divide and the east ridge. The most direct way to the standard east-side line, and climbable in a day from Holden, but it depends on the Lake Chelan boat.
hazards: Loose scree and talus throughout the upper basin and on Fernow itself
Rockfall in gullies and benches, worse with other parties above
Exposed, unavoidable class 4 (occasionally low 5th) moves on the final summit block
Complex cross-country route-finding on the final approach
Afternoon thunderstorms on the open upper ridge
Boat-dependent access via Lake Chelan to Holden

wa_mount_fernow_southeast_face.name: Entiat River from Cottonwood

approachLogistics.trailhead: Entiat River Trailhead (Cottonwood, end of Entiat River Road)

wa_mount_fernow_southeast_face.notes: Up the Entiat River trail toward the Entiat Glacier and the east ridge. The longest way in, with less gain and little avalanche exposure.
hazards: Longest way in, with a long Entiat valley walk before the glacier
Entiat Glacier crossing; crevasses and glacier recession can change conditions (unconfirmed for this variant)
Loose scree and talus throughout the upper basin and on Fernow itself
Rockfall in gullies and benches, worse with other parties above
Exposed, unavoidable class 4 (occasionally low 5th) moves on the final summit block
Complex cross-country route-finding on the final approach

wa_reynolds_peak_scramble.name: Reynolds Creek Trail and the South Fork drainage
wa_reynolds_peak_scramble.notes: The short way in, and short is relative. From the road end off the Twisp River an unmaintained primitive trail climbs through forest alongside the creek for roughly three miles. Above the confluence the tread gives out and about two miles of intermittent bushwhacking through slide alder, downed timber and a boot path that comes and goes is the real crux of the day — several parties lose more time here than on the mountain. The basin above holds snow well into summer, so an axe is worth carrying even when the valley looks dry. A longer alternative comes in over War Creek Ridge from the Williams Creek side and can be strung into a loop with a neighbouring summit, but it joins the same finish. Mark the point where you leave the tread; it is easy to miss coming down.
wa_reynolds_peak_scramble.season: Mid-July to September; axe for snow
hazards: About two miles of intermittent bushwhack above the confluence through slide alder and downed timber, with a boot path that comes and goes
Deadfall and heavy brush on the lower unmaintained trail
Avalanche terrain on the approach slopes and summit gully whenever they hold snow
Loose rock and real exposure on the summit block
Breakable crust and postholing on spring ascents
Afternoon thunderstorms on this dry east-side peak
wa_reynolds_peak_scramble.baseFinding: Follow the creek trail to about 4,800 ft, where the forest opens at the confluence of the South Fork with the main creek — a real, obvious junction of two running streams, usually crossed on a downed log. That confluence is where you leave the maintained tread. Follow the South Fork drainage upward staying roughly fifty feet above the water, which keeps you out of the worst alder and log-hopping in the streambed itself. Timber thins around 5,600 ft and the drainage narrows into a ravine that opens into a broad talus and scree basin directly beneath the peak's southeast face; that basin, at roughly 5,500 to 6,700 ft depending where you stop, is the base of the climbing. From it, a gully that often holds snow well into summer leads up to a notch on the ridge above. The decoy is at the top rather than the bottom: two horns stand across a short notch, the northern one is reached first and is lower, and the true summit is the southern horn.

wa_reynolds_peak_scramble.name: Williams Lake and War Creek Ridge

approachLogistics.trailhead: Williams Creek Trailhead (West Twisp River Road)

wa_reynolds_peak_scramble.notes: Longer, but on good trail at first and far more scenic. From the Williams Creek trailhead on the West Twisp River road at about 2,800 ft, follow the well-marked trail to Williams Lake at about 6,500 ft, then climb over Williams Butte and follow War Creek Ridge toward Camel's Hump. Drop through a boulder break in the cliffs into the upper South Fork Reynolds Creek basin and climb heather and scree to the summit pyramid.
hazards: Longer day with big elevation gain via Williams Lake and over Williams Butte and War Creek Ridge
Drop through a cliff-band boulder break into the upper South Fork basin; route-finding needed
Avalanche terrain on the summit gully whenever it holds snow
Loose rock and talus on the upper gully and Class 3-4 summit block
Lingering snow in the summit gully through early summer
Afternoon thunderstorms on this dry east-side peak

wa_diamond_in_the_rough.name: Bedal Creek to the Southwest Face basin
wa_diamond_in_the_rough.notes:
Bedal Creek is the preferred trailhead for this side of the peak because it avoids the river fords. FR 4096 off the Mountain Loop Highway, about 18.25 miles south of Darrington and roughly a mile south of Bedal Campground; the spur is rough and narrow. Trailhead about 2,790 ft.

Bedal Creek Trail #705 through old growth and along the creek's steep banks until the tread ends at a large washout, roughly one and a half to two and a half miles in. Scramble the washout to a cairned exit onto the climbers' path, which leaves left near 48.0560, -121.3631 around 3,500 ft under pink flagging and switchbacks steeply up to about 4,900 ft. Talus and meadow then lead to the 5,300 ft Bedal-Sloan saddle — last reliable water before the wall.

The Cougar Creek / North Fork Sauk alternative from FR 49 reaches the same basin from the north but requires fording the North Fork Sauk plus a cold Cougar Creek crossing, slide alder and devil's club. Either way this is a full day of walking before a long rock route.
hazards: Large washout with loose boulders and blowdown at the end of the maintained trail
Brush and real route-finding in the forest band
North Fork Sauk ford if approaching from FR 49
Long committing day — the base alone is most of a full day's walking
wa_diamond_in_the_rough.baseFinding: From the saddle, cross the low connecting ridge into the Southwest Face basin and its meadows rather than continuing onto the glacier. The base of the wall is gained from meadow and talus, dry-shod. Stepping onto glacier ice means you are on the Corkscrew approach, not this one.

wa_alpine_lookout_round_mountain_trail.name: Round Mountain Trail #1529 to Nason Ridge and the lookout spur
wa_alpine_lookout_round_mountain_trail.notes: From the highway just past the rest area, turn north onto the unsigned Butcher Creek Road (Forest Road 6910) — the turn is on a curve with fast traffic, so watch for it — and follow good gravel a few miles before turning onto the short spur that ends at the Round Mountain Trailhead. Round Mountain Trail #1529 climbs steeply for about a mile and a half through forest and an older burn to its junction with Nason Ridge Trail #1583. Turn left and west and follow the ridge trail, which undulates along the crest for a few miles to the lookout spur. A longer alternative reaches the same ridge trail from the west via the Merritt Lake trail, used mainly for through-hikes or when this side is inaccessible.
wa_alpine_lookout_round_mountain_trail.season: Roughly July through October once the ridge melts out; the lookout is one of the few in the range still staffed.
hazards: The turn off the highway is on a blind curve with fast traffic
The ridge trail narrows to a knife edge with steep rock-filled gullies dropping away on both sides
The crest is exposed to weather with no shelter along it
The lower trail climbs steeply through burn with little shade or water
wa_alpine_lookout_round_mountain_trail.baseFinding: A '9' nailed to a tree is the marker, and the knife edge is the confirmation. Walking west along Nason Ridge Trail #1583, the crest pinches down to a ten-foot-wide knife edge with steep, rock-filled gullies falling away to the highway on the south and into the river drainage on the north — that narrowing is Ninemile Saddle, and a sign carrying the numeral 9 is fixed to a tree there. It is the only labelled feature on this stretch of ridge. A few hundred yards past the saddle the trail forks: the Nason Ridge trail drops left toward Merritt Lake, and the lookout trail stays right and climbs the last traverse to the staffed lookout on the summit. The negative marker is simple: if you are losing height off the crest toward Merritt Lake and no building has come into view, you took the left fork and should go back to the junction just past the narrow section with the numbered tree.

wa_fifth_of_july_mountain_scramble.name: Basalt Ridge crest to Fifth of July Pass
wa_fifth_of_july_mountain_scramble.notes: This is the shorter alternative to the Entiat River approach. From the Basalt Pass trailhead, climb to the pass — the small stream in the gully below it is the last water, and there is none at all beyond — then follow the ridge north. The trail bypasses the first high point about 300 ft below it, and beyond the trail fork the tread fades into slick pumice. Continue north past the neighbouring tower's saddle, then through a col around 7,480 ft on the next peak's southwest ridge, dropping through a scree gully into the basin west of it. Hop the massive boulders in that basin, cross a small larch meadow, and regain the ridge. The peak can also be reached from the Entiat River side by way of Myrtle Lake, the Larch Lakes and Cow Creek Pass — that is the line the main approach and waypoints describe; the marks below are written for this Basalt Ridge side.
wa_fifth_of_july_mountain_scramble.season: Mid-July through early October, and popular in early autumn for the larch.
hazards: No water beyond the stream in the gully below Basalt Pass
Slick pumice where the ridge trail fades out
Scree gully descent off the col and a 500 ft loss into the boulder basin that must be regained
Loose rock and tree debris on the south ridge
Long open ridge fully exposed to afternoon weather
Lingering snow on north-facing terrain into early July
Remote, unreliable cell coverage
wa_fifth_of_july_mountain_scramble.baseFinding: A larch forest and then Fifth of July Pass is the gateway to the south ridge. After the boulder basin and the small larch meadow put you back on the ridge, the ground drops gradually and you walk through a larch forest immediately before arriving at Fifth of July Pass — that named saddle is where the south ridge begins, and the larch immediately below it is the confirmation. From the pass the south ridge is straightforward, with tree debris to avoid, and a short traverse along a long, broken ridgetop reaches the high point. The negative marker is the neighbouring tower: Devils Smoke Stack is a separate and harder summit with a sheer north side, climbed by steep gullies on its south with two tall steps of choss, and it lies on the far side of the intervening peak. You cannot arrive at one thinking it is the other without crossing that peak in between — so if the ground ahead rears into a tower with sheer cliffs on its north and no walkable line, you are back at the Smoke Stack rather than on this mountain's long broken crest.

wa_fifth_of_july_mountain_scramble.name: Entiat River and Larch Lakes
camps: Cottonwood Camp and the Entiat River road campgrounds
wa_fifth_of_july_mountain_scramble.notes: From the trailhead at the end of the Entiat River road, follow the Entiat River trail up the valley and climb the side trail to the Larch Lakes meadows. From a camp between the lakes the summit is a modest day out along the ridge. Longer than the Basalt Ridge line, but on maintained trail with water, so it suits multi-day trips and loops.
hazards: Burned and downed timber on the lower Entiat River and Cow Creek Meadows trails
Footbridge gone at the river crossing near the 4-mile mark
Open unmarked cross-country routefinding above Cow Creek Meadows
Loose talus and scree on the summit slopes
Sun exposure and limited water on the steep final trail mile into the meadows
Lingering snow on north-facing terrain into early July
Remote, unreliable cell coverage
wa_fifth_of_july_mountain_scramble.whyThisWay: For a multi-day trip or loop, since it keeps to maintained trail with water and lets you camp at the lakes, though it is longer than the ridge line.

wa_switchback_mountain_scramble.name: Foggy Dew Creek and Merchants Basin to Cooney Lake
wa_switchback_mountain_scramble.notes: Most parties backpack in and camp at one of the lakes rather than push the whole eighteen to twenty mile round trip in a day. From the Foggy Dew road end the trail climbs the North Fork past a two-tiered cascade — the last easy water before the country opens — and tops out of the timber into a wildflower basin below the ridge, where a spur trail branches toward the lake. An alternative comes in on the Crater Creek and Eagle Lake trail, taking a signed cutoff south past a second set of lakes to reach the same lake basin. Above the lake the ground is dry, so fill there. Larches turn gold around the basin in late September, which is a fine but colder window with a real chance of early snow icing the summit blocks.
wa_switchback_mountain_scramble.season: Mid-July to early October; larch Sep
hazards: Lightning exposure on an open ridge and summit with nowhere to shelter
Loose rock and talus on the southeast ridge
Long, mostly waterless final push above Cooney Lake
Off-trail route-finding from the pass to the summit
Iced summit blocks in shoulder season
Mosquitoes in the lake basins through mid-July
wa_switchback_mountain_scramble.baseFinding: From the lake the trail keeps climbing for roughly another mile, crossing a saddle at about 7,900 ft on the peak's southeast side, and then runs into the broad southeast ridge of the mountain. The point where the tread meets that crest is the base — everything to there is walking on a path, and everything above it is off it. The ridge itself is easy and broad, so the confirmation is the last few hundred feet rather than the first: the crest steepens into a field of large, mostly stable blocks that wants hands only occasionally, with a few more exposed steps possible right at the top. The neighbour to watch for is the similar summit under a mile north along the same crest, which is a comparable height, a comparable walk and shares a lake name with this one in places — parties do link the two, but if you have walked north along easy open ridge for the better part of a mile you are on the other peak.

wa_switchback_mountain_scramble.name: Crater Creek and the Eagle Lakes side

bivy.name: Upper Eagle Lake and Horsehead Pass
bivy.notes: The hub of the southern Sawtooth and the practical base for Switchback Mountain, with Hoodoo and Raven Ridge also within reach along the crest. Access is the Gold Creek side, not the Twisp River: turn off the highway onto the North Fork Gold Creek road, then a signed spur for several miles to the Eagle Lakes trailhead at about 4,760 ft. It is roughly 12.5 miles round trip to Upper Eagle Lake at 7,110 ft with only about 2,350 ft of gain, so it is a gentle carry by the standards of this range. Lower Eagle Lake at about 6,490 ft is the quieter option. Horsehead Pass at roughly 7,540 ft sits just above camp and is the gateway both to Boiling Lake on the far side and to the ridge walking that reaches Switchback. Linking on to Martin Lakes and Cooney Lake makes a longer circuit that takes in more of the southern summits. Season is roughly July into October; the pass holds snow on its north side later than the approach suggests. Be aware that Upper Eagle can be crowded and noisy on a fine weekend - if you want quiet, camp at Lower Eagle or push over the pass.
bivy.water: Both Eagle Lakes, and Eagle Creek is bridged on the way up. Above the lakes, on the pass and along the crest, there is nothing; carry water for any traverse day.
bivy.permit: Forest Service, no overnight permit needed. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass at the Eagle Lakes / Crater Creek trailhead. This trail is open to motorcycles and stock as well as walkers, which surprises people. Fires are restricted most summers and firewood at 7,000 ft is not a renewable resource here.
bivy.capacity: Many sites - almost every level spot around Upper Eagle Lake gets used, plus a large horse camp just below it and further sites at Lower Eagle Lake about a mile off the main trail. This is the busiest backcountry camping in the range.

wa_switchback_mountain_scramble.notes: A higher start at about 4,760 ft and a gentler grade, with a creek ford. From the Crater Creek trailhead follow the Eagle Lakes trail a little over two miles, then the Martin Creek trail to the Cooney Lake trail; parties can also base at Upper Eagle Lake and cross Horsehead Pass. Often used to make a loop with the Foggy Dew side.
hazards: Creek ford on the Crater Creek and Eagle Lakes side
Lightning exposure on an open ridge and summit with nowhere to shelter
Loose rock and talus on the southeast ridge
Dry ground above the lakes; no water on the pass or crest
Off-trail route-finding from the pass to the summit
Snow lingers on the north side of Horsehead Pass later than the approach suggests
Trail shared with motorcycles and stock
wa_switchback_mountain_scramble.whyThisWay: For a gentler grade from a higher trailhead, or to make a loop with the Foggy Dew side, at the price of a creek ford.

wa_dumbell_mountain_west.name: Phelps Creek Trail #1511 to Spider Meadow and upper Phelps Basin
wa_dumbell_mountain_west.notes:
From the Phelps Creek Trailhead at about 3,500 ft at the end of FR-6211, follow Phelps Creek Trail #1511 north up the east side of the creek. It climbs gently — roughly 1,900 ft over five or six miles — through old and second growth, with several small side streams giving reliable water the whole way. After a heavy avalanche winter the tread threads graveyards of downed timber pushed across it from the slopes to the west.

Spider Meadow near 5,150-5,400 ft is the last easy, reliable water. Walk the length of the meadow to its head, where the trail forks. The fork is unsigned: the left branch carries on toward Spider Gap and Larch Knob, and the Dumbell path is the right-hand one, an old climbers' trail into lower Phelps Basin. Most parties camp in the basin around 5,700 to 6,000 ft.

A longer alternate reaches the same basin from the east over Spider Gap from Railroad Creek and Lyman Lake out of Holden Village — used by parties already doing that loop, not as a way in.

Note that FR-6200 has been closed beyond Atkinson Flat under a storm-damage order, which blocks the drive to this trailhead entirely.
wa_dumbell_mountain_west.season: Late Jul-Sep. Before that the approach gully and the upper basin are full snow, wanting an axe and often crampons; snow returns to the upper mountain by late September
hazards: Several parallel gullies and ledge systems on the south face that look identical and do not all go — the documented way to get cliffed out here
A reported truck-sized snow block perched on a slab near 8,000 ft in the direct south-face gully
Loose rock and rubble in the gully and on the summit ledges, with parties above you
Lookalike notches and false summits near the top
FR-6200 closed beyond Atkinson Flat under a storm-damage order, which blocks the standard drive entirely
wa_dumbell_mountain_west.baseFinding:
The approach to the climbing is a creek, and it is the only way through an otherwise cliffy face. From camp in upper Phelps Basin, leave the last of the boot path and head east-north-east beside a tumbling side creek. That creek cuts the one weakness in the cliffs above the basin; the broad talus-and-scree gully on Dumbell's south side follows it. If you are working up an open face with no water beside you, you are not in the breach.

The first arrival is a notch on the south-east shoulder, around 7,900 ft, reached by climbing that gully out of the basin directly south of the summit. Grass and heather give way to talus and — through about mid-August — moderate snow.

Then comes the measurement that decides the day, and it is counted in yards rather than looked for: from the notch, go 100 to 200 yards left — west — and take the gully there. Not the gully at the notch. Aim for the right-hand side of the south face, where the easiest gully system starts. Several parallel gullies and ledge lines look alike here and they do not all go: the wrong one cliffs you out below the summit ridge.

What confirms you chose right: a little scrambling above that gully gains a system of ledges which then zig-zags up onto the West Ridge. Ledges that zig-zag rather than a continuous line, and a ridge crest at the top of them, is the confirmation. A gully that runs out against steeper rock with no ledge system is the wrong one — go back down and try further west.

The summit warning is real and it is about lookalikes: from the west ridge a few hundred feet of easy but exposed Class 3 leads to the top, and similar-looking notches and false summits near the top have sent parties astray. Keep track of which top you are on rather than assuming the first one is it.

One object to know about: a party has reported an unstable, truck-sized snow block perched on a slab near 8,000 ft in the direct south-face gully. Treat the direct line under it as loaded ground rather than a shortcut.

wa_cathedral_peak_pasayten_se_buttress.name: Andrews Creek trail #504 from the Chewuch River road
camps: Cathedral Pass benches and the tarn slabs
wa_cathedral_peak_pasayten_se_buttress.notes:
Drive north from Winthrop up the Chewuch River road to the Andrews Creek trailhead at about 3,080 ft, roughly a five-hour drive from Seattle and the shortest drive of the three ways in.

Walk Andrews Creek trail #504 up the drainage. The lower miles pass through an old burn, so there is little shade and the tread can be overgrown and wet after rain, but the creek is beside you and reliable. The trail tops out at Andrews Pass above 6,680 ft, where the burn gives way to open parkland.

Continue on the Boundary Trail #533 and drop on the Cathedral Lakes side trail to Upper Cathedral Lake at about 7,380 ft. Published figures for the whole walk from this trailhead are about nineteen miles with 5,550 ft of gain, and everyone splits it over at least two days.

Of the three trailheads this one has the shortest drive and the most walking gain; the Thirtymile trailhead is only about five and a half miles further along the same road, which makes a car shuttle between them easy.

One thing to leave alone: there is a shorter-looking approach from the Canadian side. Crossing into the United States here is illegal, the border is patrolled, and the fines are severe.
wa_cathedral_peak_pasayten_se_buttress.season: Roughly Jul-Sep; snow lingers at Andrews Pass into early July
hazards: Long approach through an old burn: little shade, overgrown wet tread
No climbers' trail to the base; navigate by the gully dividing the peak from the tower
Exposed roped climbing; loose, grainy rock on P1 and upper pitches
Hanging belay between P8 and P9 if not linked
No-fall step-across on the walk-off descent
Afternoon thunderstorms; remote, so retreat is slow
Shorter-looking Canadian approach is an illegal border crossing and patrolled
wa_cathedral_peak_pasayten_se_buttress.baseFinding: There is no climbers' trail to the base. A party who got there reported finding none and navigating purely off photographs, so stop looking for tread and navigate by the landform. The landform is the deep gully that separates Cathedral Peak from The Monk, the semi-detached tower on the lower right side of the south face. One published account leaves the maintained trail at the first switchback after Cathedral Pass and heads for the gully from there; others come across the parkland between Upper Cathedral Lake and the pass. Both end up in the same place, thirty to sixty minutes from camp. Go up into the gully — do not stop at its mouth. Three accounts put the start of the first pitch about 150 feet up the Cathedral–Monk gully, on the left wall, which is the Cathedral side. Scramble onto a tall pedestal there; it gives a decent belay stance to start from. Pedestal, left wall, about 150 feet in: that is the whole identification. How to tell this from the South Face routes, and it is a simple physical test: is there a semi-detached tower standing between you and the wall? If yes, you are at the SE Buttress, which follows the ridge behind The Monk on the right-hand edge of the south face. If you are walking up to an open face with nothing in front of it, that is the South Face route, a different and much harder climb. A related trap in the naming rather than on the ground: The Monk has its own south face with its own routes on it. Beta headed South Face may be describing the tower, not the mountain. Coming down, the descent is the walk-off to the west and then south-west back toward Upper Cathedral Lake, and its crux is a gap the route description tells you to hop across. It can be avoided by downclimbing the exposed nose beside it and stepping over — easy when dry, but no-fall ground.

wa_cathedral_peak_pasayten_se_buttress.name: Cathedral Driveway trail #510A from Loomis via Toats Coulee

bivy.name: Upper Cathedral Lake basin
bivy.notes: The working climbers' camp for both the Southeast Buttress and Amphitheater's ridges, sitting directly under the peaks with short walks to either. The basin has taken heavy use for decades and the Forest Service has posted revegetation closures on damaged ground here in the past, so treat the shoreline as off limits and camp on rock or bare dirt well back from the water. Check the posted signs on arrival rather than assuming last year's layout still applies — which sites are open has changed between seasons. Nights are cold and exposed at this elevation even in August.
bivy.water: The most dependable water anywhere on this approach — the lake holds through the season and needs no rationing. The one place on the route where you can plan on filling without checking a report first.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit from the kiosk at the Andrews Creek trailhead. No quota, no reservation, nothing to arrange in advance. Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass or a day fee to park.
bivy.capacity: A handful of established sites on slabs and benches back from the water; realistically three or four small parties before it feels crowded, and it does fill on midsummer weekends and during larch season

wa_cathedral_peak_pasayten_se_buttress.notes:
This is a trail, #510A, and not a four-wheel-drive road, despite a persistent claim to the contrary — the high-clearance warning in circulation belongs to the Iron Gate spur, a different road. Access is from Loomis by Toats Coulee Road, then a Y junction, then NF-39 and NF-300 to the trailhead at about 5,570 ft.

Be careful with the trailhead name. It appears in print as Cathedral Driveway, Chewuch, and Chewack Driveway, and the Chewuch name also belongs to a completely different trailhead near Winthrop. Navigate to the road, not the name.

The Cathedral Driveway descends from its trailhead to join the Chewuch trail #510 around mile 4.8 at about 4,300 ft, and from there it is the Chewuch valley to the Cathedral Lakes basin. Total is about seventeen and a half miles with roughly 3,700 ft of gain — the shortest walk and the least climbing of the three approaches.

The catch is at both ends. The drive is about two hours longer than from Winthrop, and because the trailhead sits high and the trail drops to meet the Chewuch, you finish the trip with roughly 1,300 ft of climbing on the way out, at the point when you least want it.
hazards: About 1,300 ft of climbing on the way out at the end of the trip
Trailhead published under several names; long extra drive
No climbers' trail to the base
Exposed roped climbing; loose, grainy rock on P1 and upper pitches
Hanging belay between P8 and P9 if not linked
Afternoon thunderstorms; remote, with a slow retreat
wa_cathedral_peak_pasayten_se_buttress.whyThisWay: When you want the shortest walk and least climbing in, and can accept a drive about two hours longer and 1,300 ft of climbing on the way out.
wa_cathedral_peak_pasayten_se_buttress.baseFinding:
The approach changes but the base does not. From camp at Upper Cathedral Lake it is the same thirty to sixty minutes: cross toward the deep gully dividing Cathedral Peak from The Monk, go about 150 feet up into the gully, and start on the left wall from a tall pedestal.

What this approach does affect is your first sighting. Coming down the Chewuch you arrive in the basin from below rather than over Andrews Pass, so take the time at the lake to pick out The Monk as a separate tower leaning against the peak's flank before walking up. The tower in front of the wall is the whole discriminator between this route and the South Face, and it is far easier to identify from across the water than from underneath.
