wa_bread_loaf.name: Silver Falls loop from the Ohanapecosh side
wa_bread_loaf.notes:
This is a single roadside boulder at about 1,900 ft in old forest, not an alpine objective, and the approach is a walk on maintained trail with essentially no gain.

From the Ohanapecosh day-use area, follow the Silver Falls Loop about a mile. The loop can also be picked up from the Grove of the Patriarchs end via the Eastside Trail, which is the alternative when work on the campground side has closed the near entrance — that corridor has been under reconstruction in recent seasons, so check which end of the loop is open rather than assuming either.

The road serving this corner of the park is seasonal: normally open from late spring through fall and gated in winter.

No climbing permit is involved. The park's climbing permit and its blue-bag rules apply to parties travelling on glaciers or above 10,000 ft, which this is not; the park entrance fee still applies.
wa_bread_loaf.season: Roughly late spring through fall, whenever the southeast corner of the park is open to vehicles
hazards: Nothing alpine; the real risks are trail closures and construction in this corner of the park
Landing on forest floor with roots and uneven ground
Seasonal road closure to the southeast entrance in winter
wa_bread_loaf.baseFinding:
The test is that you never leave the trail. The boulder sits a few feet off the Silver Falls Loop, roughly a mile round from the Ohanapecosh day-use area. If you have stepped off maintained tread, started bushwhacking, or gained more than about a hundred feet, you have walked past it — go back rather than searching uphill.

The shape is the name: a low boulder with a loaf-shaped top hold, climbed on its left side. One problem, a couple of moves.

The strongest negative is about the whole outing rather than the last hundred yards, and it is worth stating because this route is filed under the mountain: if you are on snow, on a glacier, or anywhere above a few thousand feet, you are not near this boulder and never will be. It is in low forest in the southeast corner of the park, tens of miles and twelve thousand feet from the summit routes filed beside it.

Water and escape are non-problems here — the loop has running water nearby and you can walk out either way round it. That is the honest description; do not carry mountain planning onto it.

wa_bread_loaf.name: Eastside Trail from the Grove of the Patriarchs lot

approachLogistics.trailhead: Grove of the Patriarchs parking lot (Stevens Canyon Road)

wa_bread_loaf.notes: Park at the Grove of the Patriarchs lot on the Stevens Canyon Road, cross the road to the Eastside Trail and follow it about half a mile to the Silver Falls Trail, then continue south toward the falls; the boulder is a few feet off the trail. This is the way in whenever the campground end of the loop is closed, and during that closure the loop cannot be walked through, so come back the way you went. The Grove itself stays closed behind its damaged bridge, but the lot and the Eastside Trail are open in season.
hazards: Landing on forest floor with roots and uneven ground
Grove of the Patriarchs closed behind a damaged bridge; stay on the open Eastside Trail
Loop cannot be walked through while the campground end is closed
Seasonal road closure to the southeast entrance in winter

wa_cathedral_peak_southwest_route.name: Andrews Creek trail #504 to Upper Cathedral Lake, then the trail toward Cathedral Pass
wa_cathedral_peak_southwest_route.notes:
Drive north from Winthrop up the Chewuch River road to the Andrews Creek trailhead at about 3,050 ft and walk trail #504 up the drainage to Andrews Pass above 6,680 ft. The lower half is an old burn with no shade and brushy tread. From the pass, drop into the next drainage and take the Cathedral Lakes trail up to Upper Cathedral Lake at about 7,380 ft. That is the base camp and it is a full long day of walking, usually two.

One early-season bonus is worth planning around: the chasm that splits the summit rocks is often snow-filled early, which makes the first step-across easy or trivial. Late season means a bare hole and the pure version of the move. It can snow here in any month, so carry layers whatever the forecast says.

The alternatives are the valley trail from the Thirtymile trailhead, gentle but longer, and the Cathedral Driveway trail from the high trailhead above Loomis (not the longer Iron Gate route), which walks least but drives longest and leaves you 1,300 ft of climbing on the way out.
wa_cathedral_peak_southwest_route.season: July to mid-September; the sunny south-west aspect melts out first
hazards: Old burn on the Andrews Creek trail: no shade, brushy tread; a full long day to Upper Cathedral Lake
Severe fall exposure at the summit chasm step-across; harder descending than ascending; second step-across never has snow
Loose blocks and sandy slopes between Cathedral Pass and the summit; ducks and cairns are the only markers
Snow, verglas or fresh snow possible in any month at 8,600 ft
Lightning on the local high point in afternoon convection
No cell coverage and a 17+ mile evacuation; bears and mosquitoes in the basin
wa_cathedral_peak_southwest_route.baseFinding:
This route has no rock start to find. It begins where you leave the trail, and that spot is defined by the pass, not by a cairn: walk about 0.6 mile of trail from Upper Cathedral Lake toward Cathedral Pass and step off just short of the pass at roughly 7,600 ft. If you have crested the pass and started descending the far side, you have gone too far — turn round.

Above that, the route confirms itself by texture, in a fixed order. First several hundred vertical feet of easy sandy slopes with no rock scrambling at all. Then ducks and cairns over coarse granite blocks and slabs, solid rock, class 2 to 3, with two minor steps that need a hand and one place where a friction push gets you over a block. If you are pulling on anything harder than that, you have wandered off the ducks.

The route then enters a hidden cleft running parallel to and just below the west ridge crest. That cleft is the strongest confirmation on the whole climb, because it cannot be seen from below and you either find yourself in it or you do not.

The last feature is the crux and it is unmistakable: a long chasm cleaving the summit rocks into a north and a south half, with a big chockstone jammed in the slot. Step onto the chockstone and mantle onto the bulge on the far side. The move is easy; the exposure is not, and most parties rig a handline with prusiks for the return. Lower down there is a cannonhole giving an easier alternative to one vertical step.

Negative marker: if at any point you are standing under a thousand-foot wall with a detached tower leaning against its lower right side, you have walked round to the south side of the mountain and you are below the technical routes, not on the walk-up.

wa_cathedral_peak_southwest_route.name: Cathedral Driveway trail #510A from Loomis via Toats Coulee
wa_cathedral_peak_southwest_route.notes: From the Cathedral Driveway Trailhead on the Toats Coulee road out of Loomis, the trail drops to join the Chewuch trail and then climbs the valley to the Cathedral Lakes basin. The eastern way in, with less climbing than Andrews Creek.
hazards: About 1,300 ft of climbing on the way out at the end of the trip
Severe fall exposure at the summit chasm step-across; harder descending
Loose blocks and sandy slopes between Cathedral Pass and the summit; route marked by ducks and cairns only
Snow, verglas or fresh snow possible in any month
Lightning on the local high point in afternoon convection
No cell coverage and a long evacuation; bears and mosquitoes in the basin
wa_cathedral_peak_southwest_route.whyThisWay: When you want the shortest walk and least climbing in, and can accept a much longer drive from Loomis and a climb out at the end.

wa_cathedral_peak_southwest_route.name: Thirtymile Trailhead and the Chewuch River trail toward Remmel Lake

approachLogistics.trailhead: Thirtymile Trailhead (end of the Chewuch River Road)

wa_cathedral_peak_southwest_route.notes: Follow the Chewuch River trail north from the Thirtymile Trailhead nearly to Remmel Lake, then climb to the Cathedral Lakes basin. A longer way round than Andrews Creek, used when combining the Remmel Lake country with the climb.
hazards: Longer valley walk on the Chewuch trail
Severe fall exposure at the summit chasm step-across; harder descending

wa_jack_mountain_north_ridge.name: Ross Lake to May Creek and the Nohokomeen Glacier
wa_jack_mountain_north_ridge.notes: A genuinely remote three-day outing on a mountain that sees almost no traffic, and the approach is the hard part of it. Parties reach May Creek Camp on the east shore of Ross Lake at about 1,600 ft either by walking seven or eight flat miles of the East Bank Trail from SR 20 or, far more often, by taking the resort water taxi, which removes nearly all of that. From the lake it is a few thousand feet of steep forest, and the trick is finding the open timber rather than fighting brush: parties who get it right leave the trail in open forest a couple of hundred yards from the junction, angle left of the fall line, and follow game trails through the rock bands between roughly 3,500 and 4,100 ft, where a short cliff step sometimes carries webbing left behind by earlier parties. Reaching the ridge crest around 5,000 ft, traverse to the top of the moraine, pass under the toe of the Nohokomeen Glacier and climb slabs on its left side to camp at about 6,700 ft. Some parties push on and camp higher on the glacier near 7,400 ft. The glacier above is usually straightforward and largely crack-free to its top at about 8,000 ft. Most parties climb this ridge and descend the East Ridge, which turns the trip into a traverse and puts the exit out to Jerry Lakes and the Crater Mountain trail rather than back down the timber.
hazards: Serac fall off the Nohokomeen Glacier onto the ground below its toe
Loose, fractured chert throughout with little that holds protection
Steep forest with cliff bands on the approach, far worse to descend than to climb
Wet slabs and a low fifth-class pitch where the glacier meets the ridge
Big exposure on the knife-edge crest and the snow traverse below the summit tower
Crevasses low on the glacier, and a moat where snow meets rock late season
Very remote, several days from a road with no realistic quick rescue; the usual East Ridge descent is sustained loose class 4
wa_jack_mountain_north_ridge.baseFinding: Nobody climbs this ridge from its toe; you meet it partway up off the Nohokomeen Glacier, and exactly where to leave the ice is unsettled, so treat the aiming points below as the frame and read the ground. Climb the glacier up its centre, passing just to the right of the large rock that stands out on the ice, and head for the crest to the left of the summit tower rather than for the tower itself. The glacier runs out against rock at about 8,000 ft. The one unmistakable feature on the route is there: a hole clean through the rock, a keyhole big enough to squirm through, and that hole is how the crest is gained. Parties travelling in both directions have used it as their marker. Taken from the very top of the glacier the exit costs a pitch of wet, junky low fifth class and a scramble over greasy slabs, and the party who did it that way came away convinced an easier line onto the crest exists a little lower down, short of the glacier's top edge, so it is worth traversing under the rock and looking rather than forcing the highest weakness. Above the keyhole the confirmation is instant and unlike anything below it: a knife-edged crest of genuinely solid rock, which is rare on this mountain. If what is under your hands is fractured and rotten, you are not on the crest yet. One decoy matters. The north side's other line, the headwall, rises off the same glacier and tops out within minutes of the summit, so if the snow you are on runs straight to the top with no ridge left to travel, you are on the headwall and not this route. The North Ridge leaves the ice well below the summit and still has a long way to go: knife edge, then an exposed snow traverse south across and below the summit tower with occasional protection along the upper moat, and a final pitch of low fifth class up the East Ridge to the top at 9,066 ft.

wa_jack_mountain_north_ridge.name: East Bank Trail on foot to May Creek

bivy.name: May Creek Camp, Ross Lake
bivy.notes: Designated camp on the East Bank Trail about 8 miles from the East Bank trailhead, where climbers leave the trail for the north side of Jack Mountain. It can also be reached by water taxi. Used as a first night or as the camp on the way out.
bivy.water: Ross Lake and May Creek; treat
bivy.capacity: Designated lakeshore camp with several tent sites

wa_jack_mountain_north_ridge.notes: Walk the East Bank Trail from SR-20 north along the east shore of Ross Lake to May Creek Camp, where climbers leave the trail. Several hours of flat walking each way, but it needs no booking and works whenever the highway is open.
objHaz: steep timber and cliff bands on the approach
hazards: Several flat miles of lake trail each way before the climb begins: a long, committing trip with no quick way out
Steep forest with cliff bands above May Creek, hard to navigate in the dark and far worse to descend
Serac fall off the Nohokomeen Glacier onto the ground below its toe; crevasses low on the glacier
Loose, fractured rock on the ridge with little that holds protection
Big exposure on the knife-edge crest and the snow traverse below the summit tower
Very remote with no realistic quick rescue
wa_jack_mountain_north_ridge.whyThisWay: When the water taxi is not running or booked, such as before early June, or a party prefers not to depend on a pickup; costs several hours of flat walking each way.

wa_lake_mountain_pasayten_scramble.name: Lake of the Woods camp and the east ridge
camps: Lake of the Woods and the Eureka Falls camp
wa_lake_mountain_pasayten_scramble.notes: There is no trail on the mountain itself; the whole climb is talus, scree and boulder-field walking off a high camp. The usual staging is a camp around 6,600 ft near Lake of the Woods, reached over Pistol Pass on the long-abandoned Pistol Ridge tread out of the Monument Creek valley. That approach has been unmaintained for decades and involves an unbridged ford of Eureka Creek that runs thigh to waist deep during snowmelt. A longer alternative from the Slate Pass road end reaches the same country by way of the Ferguson Lake trail and avoids that ford, at the cost of tread that is harder still to follow. From camp the peak is a couple of hours each way for a fit party, and most parties pair it with Monument Peak.
hazards: Unbridged ford of Eureka Creek: thigh to waist deep in snowmelt (June to early July)
Abandoned, unmaintained tread on Pistol Ridge with heavy deadfall and brush, faint and followed by cairns
No reliable water between the Eureka Creek ford and the Lake of the Woods basin
Loose talus near the summit and on the ridge crest
Short exposed class 3 blocky granite on the east ridge; steep north wall and northeast face off the standard line
Late snow on the last few hundred feet
No cell service, bear habitat, multi-day self-rescue distance
wa_lake_mountain_pasayten_scramble.baseFinding: From camp near Lake of the Woods, head uphill out of the lake basin toward the peak, which rises directly above camp. The base is where the open slope steepens toward the summit, and the mountain tells you where that is by refusing the obvious line. A subsidiary rock knob blocks a direct ascent from the south, and a cliff band bars a straight finish near 8,000 ft, so if you are looking up at a clean unbroken slope from the south side you are not below the standard start and pushing on will cliff you out. Bend instead onto the mountain's lower east ridge. That ridge is identifiable at its foot by larch: the lower slopes are studded with scattered larch groves, and the climbing proper begins where the larches thin out around 7,800 ft and the ground turns to boulder-hopping and coarse scree. Several gullies of much the same difficulty run up from there and any of them will go; take the one where hands come out only occasionally and the footing stays blocky rather than sliding. Early sections often feel like a staircase of granite blocks, which is a good sign you are on the ridge rather than in a scree runnel beside it. Two warnings on where not to be. The north wall and the northeast face are appreciably steeper and are not part of this route, so if the ground ahead drops away rather than rising, move back south. And the last few hundred feet hold snow late; footprints in it are a reasonable line but not proof of a good one.

wa_lake_mountain_pasayten_scramble.name: Slate Pass and the Pasayten side
wa_lake_mountain_pasayten_scramble.notes: Start high at Slate Pass on the Harts Pass road and drop toward the Middle Fork Pasayten, then work east by Eureka Creek and around into the basin below the peak. Longer and more cross-country than Pistol Pass, but it starts thousands of feet higher.
hazards: Long trail approach from Slate Pass to Robinson Creek, then an unmaintained, hard-to-follow Ferguson Lake trail
High-water fords of the Middle Fork Pasayten River during snowmelt, dangerous in June
Open avalanche chute on the Ferguson Lake trail
Loose talus near the summit and on the ridge crest
Short exposed class 3 blocky granite on the east ridge; steep north wall and northeast face off the standard line
No cell service, bear habitat, multi-day self-rescue distance
wa_lake_mountain_pasayten_scramble.whyThisWay: When starting high from the Harts Pass road to avoid the long Monument Creek valley, accepting longer, more cross-country travel and tread that is harder to follow.

wa_mount_ballard_south.name: Mill Creek and the Azurite Pass side
wa_mount_ballard_south.notes: This is the approach the peak is normally catalogued under and the one that pairs naturally with Azurite. It runs from Highway 20 up Canyon Creek and then Mill Creek on tread that has seen little maintenance since the mine closed, where slide alder and downed timber are the recurring complaint and parties routinely lose the path entirely for stretches. A longer alternative from the West Fork Methow trailhead reaches the same country by way of the Pacific Crest Trail and Horse Heaven Camp and is often preferred for combined trips despite the extra mileage. Camp is usually made near the old mine or in the basin above it. Note that the point long marked on maps as Mount Ballard is a lower north sub-summit; the true high point lies about 1,100 ft further south and is slightly higher.
hazards: Slide alder and downed timber on an unmaintained approach trail; the path is often lost
Route-finding through brush pockets and broken gullies on the flank
Loose, rotten rock and exposure near the summit ridge
Snowfields into July that can require an ice axe
Open upper mountain with full lightning exposure
Very remote, with a long and difficult evacuation if injured
wa_mount_ballard_south.baseFinding: On this side the walking ends at the old Azurite Mine site around 4,440 ft and the brush begins immediately. The base of the climb is the open basin at roughly 6,600 ft above and east of the mine, sitting between Ballard and the ridge running out toward Azurite. You know you are in it when the timber gives out and you can see the peak's flank in one piece above you rather than through trees. That flank is the difficulty: it is not a single clean face but a patchwork of brush pockets, rock ribs and short gullies, and parties consistently find that the hard part of the day is not the scrambling but picking which gully continues, a decision that comes to a head around 7,400 ft. Read the ground rather than committing early, because a gully that closes out costs a long reversal. The obvious-looking answer is a trap: the south ridge presents as a clean continuous line from below and is blocked higher by a notch with a gendarme in it, so a party that racks up the ridge crest on sight will be turned around. The other check is on which summit you are heading for. There are two high points on this mountain, and the northern one, the one carrying the old survey mark, is the lower; keep working south along the crest until the ground stops rising. If you find yourself on the connecting ridge with Azurite you have gone north and are on the wrong end of the massif.

wa_mount_ballard_south.name: South Fork Slate Creek and the east ridge

approachLogistics.trailhead: South Fork Slate Creek road end (over Harts Pass)

wa_mount_ballard_south.notes: The other side of the mountain, approached from the Slate Creek road system rather than from Mill Creek, and the line most parties who climb this peak actually use. It is shorter, the forest below camp is comparatively brush-free, and the route-finding above camp is far more legible than on the Mill Creek side, at the cost of one genuinely steep step low down and some exposed ledge work near the top. Snow conditions change this route's character completely: a filled-in slot low down and firm snow in the upper cirque make for fast travel, while dry late-season conditions leave loose rock and slippery vegetation. Camp is normally made in a scree basin below the east ridge.
hazards: Steep vegetated step through the lowest cliff band, the hardest ground on the route
Exposed ledge traverse above the high saddle
Loose rock in the summit gully with a party stacked below
Steep snow in the east cirque into midsummer
Full lightning exposure on the open upper mountain
Very remote, with a long and difficult evacuation if injured
wa_mount_ballard_south.whyThisWay: When a shorter, less brushy approach with clearer route-finding is wanted and the Slate Creek road is passable; snow in the upper cirque speeds travel.
wa_mount_ballard_south.baseFinding: The approach has one unmistakable marker and the climb has another. Start at the locked gate on the Slate Creek road at about 3,800 ft and walk the South Fork road for roughly a mile and a half to an old vehicle bridge at about 4,000 ft; that bridge is the single positive check on the whole road walk, and if you have not crossed it you are still on the main branch. From the bridge, head south through open, brush-free forest for another mile and a half or so to a scree basin around 4,800 ft, the usual camp. From camp the route climbs through tight forest and then open scree to a shoulder on the east ridge at roughly 6,200 ft. The base of the real climbing is right there and it is easy to identify because it is the wrong colour: a steep slot of heather and grass cutting through the lowest cliff band, green vegetation in an otherwise rocky wall, and the only weakness in that band. It is the steepest ground on the route and it is the crux. Bare rock gullies to either side look more like a climb and are harder and looser, so the vegetated slot is the line. Above it stay on the rib and follow the ridge crest, then the scree slope and east cirque, to a high saddle north of the summit. From that saddle do not go straight up; traverse ledges, some of them exposed, to a narrow gully that gains the summit block.

wa_mount_ballard_south.name: West Fork Methow and the PCT
wa_mount_ballard_south.notes: Up the West Fork Methow to the Pacific Crest Trail and over to the Mill Creek side. Longer, and usually chosen for combined trips.
hazards: Long approach up the West Fork Methow to the Pacific Crest Trail and over to the Mill Creek side
Slide alder and downed timber on the unmaintained Mill Creek approach
Route-finding through brush pockets and broken gullies on the flank
Loose, rotten rock and exposure near the summit ridge
Snowfields into July that can require an ice axe
Full lightning exposure; very remote with a long, difficult evacuation
wa_mount_ballard_south.whyThisWay: On a combined trip with neighbouring peaks, since the trail and Pacific Crest Trail avoid the overgrown Mill Creek tread at the cost of extra mileage.

wa_monument_peak_pasayten_scramble.name: Lower Monument Basin and the left-angling ramp
camps: Lake of the Woods and the Eureka Falls camp
wa_monument_peak_pasayten_scramble.notes: Monument is the most rugged thing in this group and sits nearly as an island, with Eureka Creek wrapping three sides of it. The travelled approach is the Monument Creek trail from the Lost River road: well maintained through old growth for about four miles to the Eureka Creek confluence, then unmaintained, brushy and deadfall-choked, with a ford of Eureka Creek that can run thigh to waist deep in early summer. From there the abandoned tread climbs onto Pistol Ridge and over Pistol Pass, and most parties camp near Lake of the Woods. Three other approaches exist off Slate Pass and Buckskin Ridge by way of the Ferguson Lake trail and reach the same basin from the north. Summit day is long enough that finishing the last talus by headlamp is common.
hazards: Loose blocky talus on the whole upper mountain
Exposed scrambling on the final summit block, Class 3 or harder
Snowfield below the summit that can hold firm or icy into midsummer
Eureka Creek ford, cold and high with early-season snowmelt
Faint, unmaintained tread beyond Pistol Pass, worse on the return
Long, remote, multi-day approach with no cell service
Afternoon thunderstorms common in this rain-shadow climate
wa_monument_peak_pasayten_scramble.baseFinding: The base of the climb is marked by water, which is convenient because you should be stopping there anyway. From high camp, traverse northwest to the saddle below Lake Mountain around 7,400 ft, then drop into Lower Monument Basin at roughly 6,100 ft. The outlet creek running from the lake in that basin is the last dependable water on the peak and it sits directly beneath the route; late in the season it can shrink to a trickle but the drainage is still obvious. Fill bottles, then look up and to the left for a ramp system that angles left across the face above you. That ramp is the start of the climbing and it is the feature to identify: it is a continuous weakness slanting up and left, not a gully, and it delivers you onto the south ridge crest at about 6,900 ft. Once you are on the crest the ground flattens into a broad talus highway that runs for well over a mile toward the summit, and that flatness is itself the confirmation that you gained the ridge in the right place rather than on a side rib. Two things mislead near the top. A false summit around 8,000 ft takes a short scramble and looks convincing; the true top is a distinctive leaning horn of granite, so if what you are standing on is not leaning you are not finished. And a steep snowfield sits just below the true summit well into midsummer, which can be crossed with an axe or turned on rock to its left, but should not be glissaded on the way down because it stays firm.

wa_monument_peak_pasayten_scramble.name: From Slate Pass by Robinson Creek and the Ferguson Lake trail

bivy.name: Lake of the Woods and the Eureka Falls camp
bivy.notes: This is the camp for Monument Peak and Lake Mountain and it is worth being clear that they are approached from a completely different point on the Harts Pass road than the crest peaks — the Monument Creek trailhead at about 2,400 feet, roughly seven miles up from Mazama, thirteen miles short of the pass. The route runs up the Lost River valley, crosses Eureka Creek where the bridge has been out in the past, then climbs the abandoned Pistol Ridge trail to Pistol Pass at 7,100 feet before dropping to the lake. Expect around thirty miles and thirteen thousand feet over three to four days for both summits — Monument at 8,592 feet by its south ridge, Lake Mountain at 8,371 by its east ridge, each a short steep scramble from the basin. The Pistol Ridge trail is unmaintained and route-finding through it is part of the work. An alternative for parties coming from the north is to drop off Lake Mountain into Eureka Creek and camp near the south fork, which shortens things considerably if the traverse is already underway. Late September brings the larches and cold clear nights; earlier in the summer the long dry climb to the pass is punishing.
bivy.water: The lake is dependable and so is Eureka Creek down in the valley. Between them, though, is the crux: the creek crossing about four miles in is the last certain water before an eight-mile climb gaining five thousand feet to the pass, and in a hot late-summer spell that carry is what makes or breaks the day. Fill completely at the creek.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit at the Monument Creek trailhead kiosk, no quota. No parking pass or fee is needed at this trailhead. Camping is prohibited within a hundred feet of the lake shoreline. Weed-free feed for stock, and the usual prohibition on tying animals to trees overnight.
bivy.capacity: Lake of the Woods is a small alpine basin with room for a couple of tents on the benches below Lake Mountain. The Eureka Falls site down in the valley near the confluence of the Lost River and Eureka Creek is a forested camp taking a party or two. Neither is developed.

wa_monument_peak_pasayten_scramble.notes: Gentler, though not shorter. Drop north from Slate Pass to the Robinson Creek trail along the Middle Fork Pasayten, then near the big meadow horse camp take the Ferguson Lake trail, which descends about seven miles to Eureka Creek just south of the peak. From there, pick a line up the south side or into the basin between Monument and Lake Mountain.
hazards: Long approach via Slate Pass, the Robinson Creek trail and the Ferguson Lake trail to Eureka Creek, remote with no cell service
Eureka Creek crossing near the peak, cold and high in early-season melt
Loose blocky talus on the upper mountain
Exposed scrambling on the final summit block
Snowfield below the summit into midsummer
Afternoon thunderstorms common in this climate
wa_monument_peak_pasayten_scramble.whyThisWay: When coming from the Harts Pass side to avoid the brushy, unmaintained Monument Creek trail and the Eureka Creek ford; an easier walk but not shorter, usually a two-day trip.
